title: Practice: History of the Periodic Table

questions.stem: A scientist in the 1860s discovers a new element with properties similar to silicon but with a higher atomic mass. Using Mendeleev's approach, where would they most likely place this element?

options.text: In a completely new group, since it is a new element
In one of the gaps Mendeleev left below silicon in the same group
At the end of the table after all known elements
Next to silicon in the same period

questions.explanation: Mendeleev deliberately left gaps in his periodic table for undiscovered elements. He predicted that elements with properties similar to silicon would fill the gap below it in the same group. This is exactly what happened when germanium was discovered in 1886, fitting his prediction of 'eka-silicon'.

questions.stem: Newlands' Law of Octaves worked well for lighter elements but failed for heavier ones. Which of the following best explains why his system broke down?

options.text: Heavier elements do not have any chemical properties
He did not leave gaps for undiscovered elements, forcing unlike elements into the same group
He arranged elements by atomic number instead of atomic mass
He only included metals in his arrangement

questions.explanation: Newlands assumed all elements had been discovered and forced them into groups of eight without leaving gaps. This meant that unlike elements were grouped together for heavier elements, making his pattern break down. Mendeleev's key improvement was leaving gaps for undiscovered elements.

questions.stem: The modern periodic table arranges elements by atomic number rather than atomic mass. Which situation demonstrates why this change was necessary?

options.text: Tellurium (mass 127.6) has a higher atomic mass than iodine (mass 126.9) but must come before it to maintain correct group properties
Transition metals all have similar densities

questions.explanation: Tellurium has a higher atomic mass than iodine, yet it belongs in Group 6 while iodine belongs in Group 7. Arranging by atomic number (Te = 52, I = 53) places them correctly, whereas arranging by atomic mass alone would swap their positions and put them in the wrong groups.

questions.stem: Mendeleev predicted that 'eka-aluminium' would have a density of about 6.0 g/cm³ and a low melting point. When gallium was discovered, it had a density of 5.9 g/cm³ and melts at 30°C. What does this demonstrate about Mendeleev's table?

options.text: That all predictions from the periodic table are always exactly correct
That Mendeleev could predict properties of undiscovered elements by identifying trends in known elements within the same group
That density always decreases down a group
That the table was arranged by density rather than atomic mass

questions.explanation: Mendeleev used the properties of known elements above and below the gaps in his table to predict the properties of undiscovered elements. The close match between his predictions for 'eka-aluminium' and the actual properties of gallium provided strong evidence that his periodic table was a valid model.

questions.stem: Dobereiner noticed 'triads' of elements where the middle element's atomic mass was roughly the average of the other two. If a triad contains lithium (mass 7) and potassium (mass 39), what would you predict for the middle element's approximate atomic mass?
questions.explanation: In Dobereiner's triads, the middle element's atomic mass is the average of the other two: (7 + 39) / 2 = 23. This matches sodium (Na, atomic mass 23), which sits between lithium and potassium in Group 1. This pattern helped early chemists recognise relationships between elements.
